newsitem.title: FRANCE: French film directors slam immigration laws.
newsitem.headline: French film directors slam immigration laws.

text.p: Scores of film directors called on the French people on Tuesday to disobey their country's tough anti-immigration laws and challenged authorities to bring them to trial for breaking them.
"We are guilty, every one of us, of putting up illegal foreign residents recently...We request being probed and put on trial," the 59 directors said in a statement published in the daily Le Monde.

The signatories, including award-winning directors Bertrand Tavernier and Matthieu Kassowitz, were protesting at a law requiring French citizens to report the arrival and departure of foreigners staying at their home.
A French teacher was convicted earlier this month of failing to report that she had put up a friend from Zaire. The teacher argued she was not aware that her friend's documents were not in order.

"We call upon our fellow-citizens to disobey and not submit to these inhuman laws," the film directors said in their statement, one of several recent protests against a four-year-old government crackdown on illegal immigrants.

French personalities of foreign descent who are active in the arts, sciences and entertainment plan to march to Paris police headquarters on Saturday, carrying suitcases, with a banner asking: "Our turn, when?"

The centre-right government, facing a general election next year, has been spurred into tightening admission conditions for foreign residents by the rise of the far-right National Front which advocates sending immigrants home.
The Front, whose outspoken leader Jean-Marie Le Pen polled 15 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential election, captured its fourth city in a municipal by-election in Vitrolles last weekend.

A bill to further harden the 1993 crackdown on illegal immigrants is currently being debated in parliament. It was somewhat softened by the Senate (upper house) last week and must now return to the National Assembly which had earlier toughened it and will have the final say in a second reading.
The Senate approved a provision letting the state restrict the freedom to put up a foreigner in one's private home.
Opponents had argued the provision would bring back the days of the Vichy wartime occupation when neighbours were encouraged to spy on each other.
There are about five million foreign nationals in France including about a million illegal entrants, most of them from developing countries.
The number of foreigners in the country rose by 40,000 in 1996, the same increase as last year but half the rate of the early 1990s. France passed tough legislation in 1993 to curb immigration.
